§0Part A · organisation

Organisation of the musculoskeletal system

Bones, cartilage and ligaments — one framework doing five jobs, split into a protective core and a mobile periphery.

The skeletal system is the bones of the skeleton plus the cartilages and ligaments that interconnect them — 206 bones of varied shape, size and tissue organisation.

The five functions of the skeletal system

  • Support — a framework that bears weight and anchors soft tissue.
  • Protection — hard cases around organs (skull, thoracic cage, vertebral canal).
  • Storage — a reservoir of minerals (calcium, phosphate) and lipids (yellow marrow).
  • Blood cell production — haematopoiesis in red marrow.
  • Leverage — bones act as levers, changing the magnitude & direction of muscle force.
The two divisions of the skeleton
DivisionContentsBonesJob
AxialSkull, vertebral column, sacrum & coccyx, thoracic cage80Central axis — protection
AppendicularLimbs + shoulder & pelvic girdles126Attaches limbs — movement
Memory hook

Axial = the axis (head + spine + ribcage). Appendicular = the appendages (limbs + girdles). 80 + 126 = 206.

Reasoning · why split the skeleton in two

The two divisions answer two opposite design briefs. The axial skeleton is built for stability and protection — a rigid central case (skull, vertebral canal, thoracic cage) wrapped around the brain, cord, heart and lungs, so it favours strength over movement. The appendicular skeleton is built for mobility — long bones acting as levers, slung from mobile girdles, trading some protection for reach and speed. Read a bone's division and you can predict what it's optimised for.

Clinical / real-world · bone is a living organ, not scaffolding

Two of the five jobs are why bone matters far beyond mechanics. Storage: the skeleton is the body's calcium bank — when blood calcium falls, parathyroid hormone withdraws it from bone; sustained withdrawal (or the oestrogen drop after menopause) thins bone toward osteoporosis. Blood cell production: red marrow — in adults mostly the axial bones plus the proximal femur and humerus — makes every red cell, white cell and platelet, which is why a marrow biopsy is taken from the iliac crest to diagnose leukaemias and anaemias.

Plate 0.1 shows the two divisions — the axial skeleton highlighted within the whole.

Label Key
Axial (highlighted)
Skull, vertebral column, sacrum/coccyx, thoracic cage — 80 bones.
Appendicular
Limbs + shoulder & pelvic girdles — 126 bones.
§1Part A · bone tissue

Bone tissue & cells

Two tissue textures, one repeating unit, four cell types.

Bone comes in two tissue textures: compact (cortical) — the dense outer shell — and spongy (cancellous / trabecular) — a lattice of struts that houses marrow.

Reasoning · why two textures

The two textures are the same material engineered for different loads. Compact bone forms the outer wall of the shaft, where bending and twisting stresses peak — a dense tube resists those best for the least weight. Spongy bone fills the ends, where forces arrive from many directions: its trabeculae line up along the lines of stress (a strut lattice, not a solid block), spreading load and absorbing shock while keeping the bone light. Same tissue, two structural solutions.

§1.1Compact-bone histology — the osteon

Compact bone is built from repeating cylinders called osteons (Haversian systems):

Parts of an osteon
StructureWhat it is
Central (Haversian) canalRuns up the osteon's core — carries blood vessels & nerves.
Concentric lamellaeRings of mineralised matrix around the canal.
LacunaeSmall spaces that each hold an osteocyte (labelled 7 in the module — "space for the osteocyte").
CanaliculiTiny channels connecting lacunae — let osteocytes exchange nutrients & signals.

§1.2The four bone cells

  • Osteoprogenitor cells — stem cells that divide into osteoblasts.
  • Osteoblasts — build bone: secrete osteoid (unmineralised collagen-I matrix).
  • Osteocytes — mature osteoblasts trapped in lacunae; maintain bone & sense load.
  • Osteoclasts — large cells that resorb (break down) bone.
Memory hook · the four cells

Follow the suffix: -blast = build (osteoblasts lay down osteoid), -clast = carve (osteoclasts chew bone away), -cyte = caretaker (osteocytes maintain it and sense load). Osteoprogenitor cells are the reserve pool that becomes the rest.

Reasoning · why a canal at the core

Osteocytes are walled into solid mineral, so they can't get nutrients by diffusion alone. The Haversian canal brings the blood supply into the middle of the bone, and canaliculi form a relay of tiny pipes so every osteocyte stays fed — which is why bone is living, remodelling tissue, not inert rock.

Clinical / real-world · a balance you can shift

Health is the osteoblast–osteoclast balance held even; tip it and disease follows. Runaway osteoclasts hollow out bone (osteoporosis) — which is exactly why the commonest bone drugs, bisphosphonates, work by switching osteoclasts off. The osteocytes explain the flip side: because they sense mechanical load, loaded bone is told to build itself up (Wolff's law) — weight-bearing exercise thickens bone, while bed-rest or spaceflight strips it away.

Bone develops from the mesoderm germ layer; its embryonic connective-tissue precursor is mesenchyme.

§2Part A · bone formation

Osteogenesis, growth & remodelling

Two ways to make bone, one plate that lengthens it, and a lifelong turnover.

Osteogenesis (bone development) begins from mesenchymal precursors and follows one of two routes.

Two types of ossification
EndochondralIntramembranous
RouteMesenchyme → chondroblasts → a cartilage model, later replaced by boneMesenchyme condenses → osteoblasts deposit osteoid directly (no cartilage model)
DetailChondroblasts secrete matrix & get trapped as chondrocytesOsteoblasts trapped in osteoid become osteocytes
MakesMost long bonesFlat bones (e.g. skull)
Reasoning · why two ways to build a bone

The route matches the job. Bones that must keep lengthening for years — the long bones of the limbs — are first laid down as a cartilage model (endochondral), because cartilage can grow from within and then be replaced piece-by-piece with bone, leaving a growth plate that keeps elongating the bone from inside. Bones that only need to enclose and expand — the flat plates of the skull — skip the template and ossify directly within a membrane (intramembranous), letting them grow at their margins and stay thin. Function dictates the method.

§2.1Growth in length

Bones grow in length until early adulthood at the epiphyseal plate — a thin plate of hyaline cartilage between the diaphysis and epiphysis. When longitudinal growth stops, the plate ossifies into the epiphyseal line.

Plate 2.1 shows the plate on X-ray, between the shaft and the bone's end.

Label Key
Epiphyseal plate (arrows)
Hyaline-cartilage plate between diaphysis & epiphysis — the site of growth in length.
Epiphyseal line
What the plate becomes once growth stops.

§2.2Remodelling

Bone is continuously renewed by the balance of osteoblast deposition and osteoclast resorption — reshaping bone to load and repairing microdamage.

Clinical / real-world

Tip the balance and disease follows: too much osteoclast activity (or too little osteoblast) thins bone toward osteoporosis; the growth plate is also the weak point in children, so fractures there (Salter–Harris) can disturb growth.

§3Part A · bones

Bones — classification & long-bone anatomy

Two ways to sort a bone, and the anatomy of the reference model.

Bones are classified by internal tissue organisation (compact vs spongy, §1) and by shape.

  • Long — shaft + two ends (femur, humerus): leverage.
  • Short — cube-shaped (carpals, tarsals): stability with limited gliding.
  • Flat — thin, often curved (skull, sternum, ribs): protection & broad attachment.
  • Irregular — complex (vertebrae, facial bones).
  • Sesamoid — embedded in a tendon (patella): protects the tendon & improves leverage.
Reasoning · shape is a job description

Each shape is optimised for a mechanical task, so the shape predicts the function. Long bones are levers — a stiff shaft maximises the arc a muscle can swing. Short, cube-like bones sit where you need stability with only small gliding movements (wrist, ankle). Flat bones are armour and broad muscle anchors (skull vault, sternum, ribs). Irregular bones are shaped by doing several jobs at once — a vertebra bears load, shields the cord and anchors muscles. A sesamoid (the patella) rides inside a tendon to protect it and lengthen its lever arm. Name the shape and you've named the job.

§3.1Anatomy of a long bone

Long-bone regions & coverings
PartWhat it is
DiaphysisThe shaft — compact bone around the medullary cavity.
EpiphysisExpanded end — spongy bone under a compact shell; forms the joint surface.
MetaphysisZone between them — holds the growth plate in the young.
Medullary cavityCentral space with marrow (red = blood cells; yellow = fat).
PeriosteumOuter covering: outer fibrous layer (absent on articular surfaces & sesamoids) + inner cellular layer (osteoprogenitors — key in healing/remodelling). Anchored by Sharpey's fibres; vascular & innervated.
EndosteumThin membrane lining the inner bony wall, Haversian canals & trabeculae.

Plate 3.1 labels the regions of a long bone together with its periosteum & endosteum.

Label Key
Diaphysis & epiphyses
Shaft (compact bone around the marrow cavity) + expanded ends (spongy bone under a shell); shown as 'Living' vs 'Dried'.
Marrow cavity
Red (blood-forming) & yellow (fat) marrow; articular cartilage caps the joint surface.
Periosteum
Outer fibrous + inner cellular (osteoprogenitor) layers, anchored by Sharpey's (perforating) fibres; vascular & innervated.
Endosteum
Thin membrane lining the marrow cavity, Haversian canals & trabeculae.
Clinical / real-world · why a broken bone hurts so sharply

The periosteum is richly innervated, so trauma to bone produces sharp, well-localised pain that originates from the periosteum — while the mineral interior itself has few pain fibres.

Reasoning · bones fuse with age

Infants have more than 206 bones: many start as separate pieces and fuse later. The hip bone, for instance, begins as three bones — ilium, ischium and pubis — that fuse into one at the acetabulum (Plate 3.2). Fewer, fused bones trade the flexibility of growth for adult strength.

Label Key
Ilium · ischium · pubis
Separate in the child; fuse at the acetabulum into one hip bone.
Acetabulum
Socket (lunate articular surface, fossa & notch) for the femoral head.
§4Part B · joints

Joints (articulations)

Classify by how much it moves, and by what holds it together.

A joint is where two bones meet. Two classifications overlap — functional (movement) and structural (tissue + cavity).

Functional classes
ClassMovementExample
SynarthrosisNoneSkull suture
AmphiarthrosisSlightPubic symphysis
DiarthrosisFreeSynovial joints (knee, shoulder)

§4.1Structural classes

  • Fibrous — no cavity, dense connective tissue: sutures (skull), syndesmoses (tibia–fibula), gomphoses (tooth in socket).
  • Cartilaginous — no cavity, joined by cartilage: synchondroses (primary, hyaline — e.g. growth plate) & symphyses (secondary, fibrocartilage — e.g. pubic symphysis).
  • Synovial — a fluid-filled cavity; the freely-movable joints.

Plate 4.1 contrasts the three structural families.

Label Key
Fibrous
Dense connective tissue, no cavity — e.g. a skull suture, the tooth-in-socket (gomphosis) and the radio-ulnar syndesmosis.
Cartilaginous
Bound by cartilage — a synchondrosis (e.g. the growth plate) and the pubic symphysis.
Synovial
A fluid-filled cavity — the freely-movable family, detailed in Plates 4.2–4.3.

§4.2The synovial joint

A synovial joint's parts: hyaline articular cartilage (reduces friction, absorbs shock), a fibrous capsule, a synovial membrane (makes synovial fluid that lubricates), and ligaments (bone-to-bone). Its stability comes from three things: the shape of the articular surfaces, the ligaments, and muscle tone.

Plate 4.2 labels a synovial joint; Plate 4.3 shows all six types.

Label Key
Hyaline articular cartilage
Reduces friction & absorbs shock.
Capsule + synovial membrane
Membrane secretes synovial fluid that lubricates the cavity.
Ligament / tendon
Ligament joins bone to bone; tendon joins muscle to bone.
The six synovial joint types
TypeExampleMovement
PlanarFacet (intercarpal) jointsGliding
HingeElbow, ankleOne plane (flex/extend)
PivotAtlanto-axial; proximal radio-ulnarRotation
CondyloidWrist (radiocarpal)Two planes
SaddleThumb carpometacarpalTwo planes + opposition
Ball-and-socketShoulder (glenohumeral), hipAll planes
Label Key
Planar · hinge · pivot
Gliding · one plane · rotation.
Condyloid · saddle · ball-and-socket
Two planes · two planes + opposition · all planes.

Accessory structures

  • Articular disc — fibrocartilage between articular surfaces (e.g. the knee).
  • Labrum — a fibrocartilage ring that deepens a socket (e.g. the shoulder).
  • Bursa — a fluid-filled sac that reduces friction between bone and tendon/ligament.
Reasoning · shape sets the movement

A hinge is two matched cylinders → one plane of motion; a ball-and-socket removes those constraints → every plane, but less stable (why the shoulder dislocates and a suture never does). You can predict a joint's movements from its geometry alone.

Clinical / real-world · the price of mobility

Stability and mobility trade off, and the clinic pays the bill. The shoulder — a large humeral head on a shallow socket — is the most mobile joint and therefore the most commonly dislocated. The knee, a hinge held together mainly by ligaments, tears those ligaments (the ACL) when twisted under load. And because synovial stability rests on shape + ligaments + muscle tone, losing any one of the three — a stretched ligament, a wasted quadriceps — leaves the joint unstable: exactly why rehabilitation rebuilds the muscles around a damaged joint.

§5Part B · muscle

Muscle

~700 engines — arranged for force or range, attached fixed-to-moving, and named so the name tells you what they do.

The muscular system is roughly 700 skeletal muscles. How the fascicles (fibre bundles) are arranged trades force against range.

Fascicle arrangements
ArrangementPatternExample
ParallelFascicles run the muscle's lengthSartorius
FusiformParallel but the belly bulges, tapering at the endsDigastric
CircularConcentric rings around an orifice (sphincter)Orbicularis oculi
ConvergentBroad origin converging on one tendon (triangular)Pectoralis major
PennateShort fascicles angled onto a tendon — more fibres = more force. Uni (extensor digitorum longus), bi (rectus femoris), multi (deltoid)—

Plate 5.1 shows the fascicle arrangements; Plate 5.2 the pennate sub-types.

Label Key
Parallel · fusiform
Fibres along the long axis; fusiform belly bulges.
Circular · convergent
Sphincter rings; broad origin converging on one tendon.
Pennate
Short angled fascicles → more force.
Label Key
Unipennate
Fascicles on one side of the tendon (extensor digitorum longus).
Bipennate
Both sides of a central tendon (rectus femoris).
Reasoning · why arrangement = force vs range

Fascicle arrangement is a trade between how far a muscle shortens and how hard it pulls. In a parallel muscle the fibres run the full length, so it shortens a long way (big range of movement) but has only as many fibres as its cross-section allows. A pennate muscle angles many short fibres onto a central tendon — like barbs on a feather — so you pack far more fibres into the same volume: much greater force, but less shortening. That's the whole logic — powerful muscles (deltoid, rectus femoris) are pennate; muscles built for reach and speed (sartorius) are parallel.

Origin = attachment to the stationary bone (usually proximal); insertion = attachment to the movable bone (usually distal). In a contraction the insertion is pulled toward the origin — so knowing which end is fixed tells you which way the bone will move.

Supportive connective tissue

  • Tendon — a rope attaching muscle to bone.
  • Aponeurosis — a broad flat sheet connecting muscle to muscle/bone.
  • Fascia — wraps muscles like a stocking; deep fascia forms intermuscular septa → muscle compartments.
Clinical / real-world · when fascia becomes a trap

Deep fascia is tough and barely stretches — handy for making compartments, dangerous after injury. If bleeding or swelling builds up inside a closed fascial compartment (e.g. after a fracture or crush), the unyielding fascia lets the pressure climb until it chokes the vessels and nerves passing through — compartment syndrome, a surgical emergency relieved by slicing the fascia open (fasciotomy). The very inextensibility that organises the limb is what makes it a trap.

§5.1Reading a muscle's name

Anatomists build muscle names from descriptive terms — region, position, shape, and action — so the name is a clue to the muscle.

Naming terms
RegionPosition / directionShapeAction
Abdominis (abdomen)Rectus (straight)Deltoid (triangle)Flexor / Extensor
Brachii (arm) · Capitis (head)Transversus (transverse)Teres (round, long)Abductor / Adductor
Femoris (femur) · Pollicis (thumb)Externus / Profundus (deep)Serratus (saw) · Splenius (bandage)Pronator / Supinator
Hallucis (great toe) · Inguinal (groin)Superficialis · SuperiorisLongus / Brevis · Latissimus (widest)Levator · Tensor · Rotator
Memory hook

Read the name in pieces: Flexor · pollicis · longus = "the long muscle that flexes the thumb." Extensor · carpi · radialis = "extends the wrist, on the radial side." The name is the job description.

§6Part C · upper limb

Upper limb

Regions, bones, fascial compartments, and the nerves & vessels threading through.

The upper limb is organised into regions — pectoral/clavicular/scapular and the axilla, then arm, cubital region, forearm, wrist, palm and digits (Plate 6.1).

Label Key
Pectoral / clavicular / scapular & axilla
The shoulder-girdle regions that link the limb to the trunk.
Arm · cubital · forearm
Brachium, the elbow (cubital) region, and antebrachium.
Wrist · palm · digits
The distal hand regions (dotted outlines mark each region).

§6.1Osteology

Bones, proximal → distal: clavicle, scapula, humerus, radius, ulna, carpals, metacarpals, phalanges — jointed by the elbow, proximal & distal radio-ulnar, wrist, carpometacarpal, metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints.

§6.2Fascia & compartments

Limb fascia encloses and separates muscles into compartments:

  • Superficial fascia — subcutaneous; fat + superficial vessels, nerves & lymphatics.
  • Deep fascia — continuation of the pectoral & axillary fascia: brachial fascia (arm), antebrachial fascia (forearm). Its thickenings at the wrist form the flexor retinaculum (anterior) and extensor retinaculum (posterior).

Plate 6.2 shows the fascial compartments in cross-section.

Label Key
Deep fascia
Brachial (arm) & antebrachial (forearm) fascia; intermuscular septa create compartments.
Cross-sections (B–D)
Anterior/posterior compartments; the wrist section shows the carpal tunnel & retinacula.

Transitional zones (clinically important — packed with neurovascular structures)

  • The axilla — gateway between trunk and arm.
  • The cubital fossa — the front of the elbow.
  • The carpal tunnel — under the flexor retinaculum at the wrist.
Clinical / real-world · why the transitional zones matter

Each "gateway" is crammed with nerves and vessels, so each is a clinical hotspot. The cubital fossa is where you draw blood and read a blood pressure — the median cubital vein and the brachial artery sit right there. The carpal tunnel is a rigid space under the flexor retinaculum; swell its contents and the median nerve is squeezed — carpal tunnel syndrome (tingling in the thumb-side fingers, a weak grip). The axilla holds the limb's lymph nodes, which is why they're examined and sampled when staging breast cancer.

§6.3Muscles, nerves, dermatomes & myotomes

Muscles sit in fascial compartments; hand muscles are intrinsic (both attachments in the hand) or extrinsic (proximal attachment on the humeral epicondyles/forearm, acting on forearm & hand).

Nerves come from the brachial plexus (roots C5–T1). They're mixed nerves — motor (efferent, brain → muscle) and sensory (afferent, skin/muscle/joint → cord → cortex) — bundled together in connective tissue (epineurium).

Memory hook · dermatome vs myotome

Dermatome = a strip of skin from one spinal nerve. Myotome = the muscle supplied by one spinal nerve.

Clinical / real-world · reading a nerve lesion off the map

Because each spinal nerve serves a defined strip of skin and set of muscles, the pattern of numbness and weakness pinpoints which root is damaged — a slipped disc pressing one nerve root produces numbness in its dermatome and weakness in its myotome, so the exam localises the level without a scan. The same map explains shingles, whose rash erupts along a single dermatome — the exact skin strip of the nerve where the dormant virus was hiding.

§6.4Blood supply & drainage

Arteries: subclavian → axillary (at the lateral border of the 1st rib) → brachial, which splits in the cubital fossa into the ulnar (larger) and radial (smaller) arteries → the superficial & deep palmar arches → digital arteries (Plate 6.3).

Label Key
Subclavian → axillary → brachial
Brachial splits into radial & ulnar in the cubital fossa.
Palmar arches
Superficial & deep arches → digital arteries.
Reasoning · why arches and anastomoses

Notice how the vessels keep rejoining — the two palmar arches, plus anastomoses around the scapula and elbow. These give collateral routes: if the main artery is compressed (a tourniquet, a clot) blood can detour around the block and the hand still survives. It's also why you check both the radial and ulnar supply (Allen's test) before sampling from the radial artery — you're confirming the other arch can cover it.

Veins: two sets — deep and superficial — linked by perforating veins whose valves stop backflow from deep to superficial during muscle contraction (Plate 6.4).

Label Key
Superficial
Cephalic & basilic veins.
Deep + perforators
Venae comitantes; valved perforators stop deep→superficial backflow.
§7Part D · development

How a limb is built

From a bump on the flank to a rotated, jointed limb — two mesoderms, one ridge, well-timed cell death.

Development is continuous from a totipotent zygote: embryonic period = weeks 1–8 (organs form — the vulnerable window), foetal = week 9 to birth.

Gastrulation forms the three germ layers; the entire MSK system arises from mesoderm. Limbs begin at the end of week 4, and two mesoderms divide the labour:

  • Lateral plate mesoderm → the limb's skeleton (bones & connective tissue).
  • Paraxial mesoderm (somites) → the muscle (and vascular components) that migrate in.

Each limb bud is a mesodermal core under ectoderm, capped by the apical ectodermal ridge (AER), which signals the mesoderm beneath it to keep growing — driving outgrowth shoulder-to-fingertip.

Memory hook

Lateral Plate → the Platform (skeleton). Somite → the Soft movers (muscle). Each somite splits into sclerotome (skeleton: vertebrae/ribs), myotome (muscle), dermotome (dermis).

Timeline: motor axons enter the bud in week 5; limbs rotate in week 8 (upper dorsally, lower ventrally — why elbows and knees point opposite ways); digits are freed when apoptosis deletes the tissue between the digital rays.

Reasoning · why weeks 1–8 are the danger zone

Timing is everything. During the embryonic period (wk 1–8) structures are being built from scratch — cells dividing, migrating and switching genes on in a precise order — so an insult (a teratogen, a missing signal) corrupts the blueprint itself and yields a structural malformation. After week 8 the parts already exist and mostly grow, so the same insult does far less structural harm. This is why limb defects trace back to a narrow early window — and why the AER and well-timed apoptosis matter so much: lose AER signalling and the limb truncates; skip the apoptosis and the digits stay fused.

§8Part D · when it goes wrong

Limb anomalies

Each defect is a step from §7 that failed.

Extremes: meromelia (partial absence of a limb) and amelia (whole-limb absence). Causes are genetic, teratogenic, mechanical or vascular, and the embryonic weeks 1–8 are the vulnerable window.

Common limb anomalies
AnomalyMechanism
SyndactylyFailed interdigital apoptosis (§7) — digits stay webbed (cutaneous) or fused (osseous).
PolydactylyExtra digits; inherited as a dominant trait.
Clubfoot (talipes)Multifactorial; ~1:1000 births; foot mis-positioned for weight-bearing.
AchondroplasiaFGFR3 mutation, autosomal dominant — impairs cartilage→bone conversion → short limbs.
Reasoning · every anomaly is a §7 step that failed

Read each defect back to its developmental step and the list stops being memorisation. Syndactyly = the interdigital apoptosis that normally frees the fingers never happened, so they stay webbed. Polydactyly = the outgrowth signal (an over-active AER/ZPA) duplicated a ray. Meromelia / amelia = outgrowth stalled, or never started. Achondroplasia = endochondral ossification is braked by an over-active FGFR3, so the long bones can't lengthen — short limbs on a normal-length trunk. The name of the anomaly is really the name of the process that broke.

Clinical / real-world · thalidomide

Thalidomide, sold in the late 1950s–60s as a "safe" morning-sickness drug, caused catastrophic limb defects (meromelia/amelia) when taken in early pregnancy — the defining lesson in teratology, and the reason medications are reviewed before conception (§7's vulnerable window in action).

R Recall checklist — the module
  • Skeletal functions — support, protection, storage, blood cell production, leverage. Axial 80 / appendicular 126 = 206.
  • Bone tissue — compact (osteons: Haversian canal, lamellae, lacunae, canaliculi) vs spongy. Cells: osteoprogenitor, osteoblast, osteocyte, osteoclast.
  • Ossification — endochondral (cartilage model) vs intramembranous (direct). Growth at epiphyseal plate → epiphyseal line. Remodel = osteoblast vs osteoclast.
  • Bone shapes — long, short, flat, irregular, sesamoid. Long bone: diaphysis/epiphysis/metaphysis/marrow; periosteum (Sharpey's fibres, innervated) + endosteum.
  • Joints — functional (syn/amphi/di); structural fibrous (suture/syndesmosis/gomphosis), cartilaginous (synchondrosis/symphysis), synovial. Six synovial types; stability = shape+ligaments+tone; disc/labrum/bursa.
  • Muscle — parallel/fusiform/circular/convergent/pennate; origin(fixed)/insertion(moved); tendon/aponeurosis/fascia; names encode region/position/shape/action.
  • Upper limb — clavicle→phalanges; superficial vs deep fascia (retinacula); axilla/cubital fossa/carpal tunnel; brachial plexus C5–T1 (mixed, epineurium); dermatome vs myotome; subclavian→axillary→brachial→radial/ulnar→palmar arches; deep+superficial veins.
  • Limb development — MSK from mesoderm; limbs start wk4; lateral plate → skeleton, somite → muscle; AER → outgrowth; somite → sclero/myo/dermotome; rotation wk8; digits by apoptosis.
  • Anomalies — meromelia/amelia; syndactyly, polydactyly, clubfoot, achondroplasia (FGFR3), thalidomide.
